01.actor: Rabbi Tarfon and his students, including Rabbi Yehuda
01.event: A yevama came to perform halitza before Rabbi Tarfon, who told the onlookers to answer along with the court.
01.outcome: The students recited the phrase three times, as instructed; nothing further is told.
01.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalls sitting before Rabbi Tarfon when a widow came to perform the halitza ceremony. Rabbi Tarfon told everyone present to call out the verse's phrase three times. It is a brief anecdote used to illustrate a rule, with no real turn.
01.missing: No complication or resolution; the anecdote only illustrates a practice.

02.event: Mar Ukva secretly tossed coins to a poor neighbor each day; the day the poor man came to see who it was, Mar Ukva and his wife fled and hid in a furnace.
02.turn: His feet were scorched in the still-hot furnace while hers were not, and his wife offered her unburned feet to him.
02.outcome: He was distraught, and she explained that her charity was more immediately helpful because she gave food from the home, so she was spared.
02.summary: Mar Ukva used to toss four dinars to a poor neighbor every day without being seen. One day the poor man waited to find out who it was, and Mar Ukva and his wife ran away and hid in a furnace whose fire was banked but still hot. His feet were burned, and his wife told him to rest them on hers; when he was upset, she explained that her aid reaches the poor more directly than his money does.

03.actor: Rav Giddel, Rabbi Abba, Rabbi Zeira and Rav Yitzhak Nappaha
03.event: Rabbi Abba bought a piece of land that Rav Giddel was in the middle of acquiring, and Rav Giddel complained through Rabbi Zeira to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha.
03.turn: Rav Yitzhak confronted Rabbi Abba at the Festival; Rabbi Abba pleaded ignorance and refused to sell, offering the land only as a gift.
03.outcome: Rav Giddel would not accept a gift and Rabbi Abba would not use the land since Rav Giddel had been working on it, so it stayed untouched and was called the land of the Sages.
03.summary: Rav Giddel was working to buy a plot when Rabbi Abba bought it first. Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who took it to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, who confronted Rabbi Abba at the Festival with a parable of a poor man's loaf being snatched. Rabbi Abba said he hadn't known and would not sell, only give it as a gift. Rav Giddel refused gifts and Rabbi Abba felt he could not take the land, so it stayed unused and became known as the land of the Sages.

04.event: A man brought him the first shearing of his flock while having a lawsuit pending before him; Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift and disqualified himself from the case.
04.turn: While two other scholars judged the case, he found himself mentally arguing both sides for the litigant.
04.outcome: He concluded that if he, who took nothing, was biased, then bribe-takers are certainly biased, and exclaimed against them.
04.summary: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing of his sheep. When the man admitted he also had a case, Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift and disqualified himself, seating two other scholars to judge it. As he came and went he caught himself thinking up arguments for the man, and concluded that if he was swayed without taking anything, those who really take bribes are certainly corrupted.

05.event: A case about an alleyway closed by the sea on one side and a garbage dump on the other came before him, and he gave no ruling either way.
05.outcome: He said neither permitted nor prohibited; the Gemara explains his silence.
05.summary: An alleyway had the sea at one end and a garbage dump at the other, and the question of whether it counted as enclosed was brought to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. He declined to rule either way, because the dump might be removed or the sea might recede, though the partitions currently stood.
05.missing: The case is cited as a precedent; no actors, no event beyond a non-ruling.

06.event: At the king's gate, Rav Ashi saw Mar Zutra's face go pale with craving for the food the chief butler carried past, and fed him some of it by finger.
06.turn: The butler protested that Rav Ashi had spoiled the king's meal, and Rav Ashi said the food was already defective and then pointed to the exact spot.
06.outcome: The soldiers checked that spot and found a leprous infection; Rav Ashi explained he had seen a leprous spirit hovering over it.
06.summary: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi sat at the king's gate as the king's chief butler passed with food. Rav Ashi saw Mar Zutra go pale with craving and put some of the food into his mouth, and the butler complained that the king's meal was ruined. Rav Ashi claimed the food was already unfit; when the first check found nothing he pointed to a spot, and the infection was found there. He said he had seen a leprous spirit over it.

07.event: A man did a small favor for a judge (removed a feather from Ameimar's head; covered Mar Ukva's spittle) and then said he had a case before him.
07.turn: The favor made each judge feel biased.
07.outcome: Each judge disqualified himself from hearing the man's case.
07.summary: While Ameimar was sitting in judgment, a feather landed on his head and a man removed it; when the man said he had a case, Ameimar disqualified himself. Likewise a man covered spittle lying before Mar Ukva, and when he said he had a case, Mar Ukva too recused himself.

08.actor: A man whose mother had been taken captive, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
08.event: A case came before Rabbi where a man casually mentioned that he and his mother had been captured and that his thoughts were on his mother whenever he went out for water or wood.
08.turn: His offhand remark, not formal testimony, was treated as reliable that she had stayed with him and was not defiled.
08.outcome: Rabbi allowed the mother to marry into the priesthood on the basis of his words.
08.summary: A man, speaking offhandedly, said that when he and his mother were captive among gentiles he always kept his attention on her, even while drawing water or gathering wood. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi accepted this incidental remark and permitted her to marry a priest.

09.actor: A man from Eretz Yisrael and Rabbi Hanina
09.event: A man whose brother's widow lived in Babylonia asked Rabbi Hanina whether he could go there to marry her.
09.turn: Rabbi Hanina sharply answered that the brother had married a foreign woman and died.
09.outcome: Rabbi Hanina implied the man should not follow his brother out of Eretz Yisrael.
09.summary: A man in Eretz Yisrael was obligated in levirate marriage to his late brother's widow, who lived in Babylonia, and asked Rabbi Hanina if he could go down to marry her. Rabbi Hanina answered that his brother had married a Samaritan and died, thank God, and asked whether he wanted to follow him there. The man was in effect refused.

10.missing: The passage is Rava's rule about judges fixing a location, plus a report that Rav Pappa and Rav Huna held halitza before five judges and the legal explanation; no event with a turn.

11.event: Ben Nappaha owned houses in five courtyards in Usha and a case came before the Sages about whether he prohibited carrying in all of them.
11.outcome: The Sages ruled that only his actual residence prohibits carrying.
11.summary: A man named ben Nappaha had houses in five courtyards in Usha, and the Sages were asked whether this required an eiruv in each. They ruled that only the place where he actually lived prohibited carrying.
11.missing: A bare legal precedent; no personal drama or turn.

12.actor: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin and Rabbi Ami
12.event: They bought a maidservant for small coins, put up a piece of silver as collateral because they had no cash, and she then rose in price.
12.turn: The sellers wanted out of the sale and the case went to Rabbi Ami.
12.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled there was no payment and no valid collateral, so no sale took place.
12.summary: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin agreed to buy a maidservant but, lacking the coins, left a silver piece as collateral. When her price went up the sellers backed out and they brought the dispute to Rabbi Ami, who ruled that neither coins nor collateral had been validly given, so they had not acquired her.

13.event: He ruled a child fit (not a mamzer) when a woman's husband went overseas and she gave birth after twelve months.
13.turn: The Gemara challenges whose opinion he followed.
13.outcome: The ruling is defended in the next segment as following the majority.
13.summary: A woman's husband went overseas and she bore a child after twelve months. Rava Tosfa'a ruled the child legitimate, and the Gemara asks how, since this follows a minority opinion about delayed births.
13.missing: The case is only a halakhic precedent being challenged; the details of the woman and child are absent.

14.event: Bonyos sent Rabbi a measuring vessel said to be an ancient se'a, and Rabbi measured it.
14.outcome: He found it held 217 eggs, which does not match known se'a measures.
14.summary: Bonyos sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a se'a-measure from Na'usa, and Rabbi measured its capacity at 217 eggs.
14.missing: The significance and any resolution of the mismatch; it is a measurement report.

15.actor: Rav Sheshet and a man passing his father-in-law's house
15.event: Rav Sheshet lashed a man who merely passed by his father-in-law's door.
15.turn: The Gemara objects that mere passing should not be punished.
15.outcome: It explains that this man was suspected with his mother-in-law.
15.summary: A man passed by the entrance to his father-in-law's house and Rav Sheshet had him flogged. The Gemara explains that he was rumored to be involved with his mother-in-law.
15.missing: No detail of the incident beyond a legal precedent.

16.event: A groom claimed he found no blood on the wedding night, and the bride said she was a virgin; Rabban Gamliel had the cloth brought to him.
16.turn: He soaked and washed the cloth and found drops of blood on it.
16.outcome: He told the groom to go take his bride, since she was a virgin.
16.summary: A groom came to Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi saying he had not found blood, while the bride insisted she was a virgin. Rabban Gamliel asked for the cloth, soaked and laundered it, and found drops of blood. He told the groom to go take his purchase.

17.actor: The daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon
17.event: The Sages set aside four hundred gold coins for her perfume allowance for a single day.
17.turn: She answered them with a wish that they should do the same for their own daughters.
17.summary: When the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon was granted four hundred gold coins for perfume for one day, she said to the Sages that they should pledge that for their own daughters, and they answered Amen.

18.actor: A debtor's buyer and a creditor
18.event: A creditor repossessed one of two plots a debtor had sold, then came to repossess the second.
18.turn: The purchaser of the second plot took one hundred dinars to the creditor and offered it in exchange for giving up both claims.
18.outcome: The creditor's response is not shown here; the text moves to the legal question of what is written in the repossession document.
18.summary: A man owed one hundred dinars and had sold two plots for fifty each. The creditor took one from its buyer, then came for the other. That buyer went to him with one hundred dinars and offered him the money to give up his claims on both.
18.missing: What the creditor did in response.

19.actor: A dying man, his heirs, and Rav Ashi
19.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter and died leaving only two half-shares of palm trees, and the heirs wanted to give her those.
19.turn: Rav Ashi questioned whether people call two halves a palm tree; Rav Mordekhai relayed a tradition from Rava that they do.
19.outcome: The heirs may fulfill the bequest with the two halves.
19.summary: A man promised his daughter a palm tree but at death owned only two half-shares in different trees. Rav Ashi wondered whether that counts, and Rav Mordekhai relayed Rava's view that people call two halves a palm tree, so the heirs could give the halves.
19.missing: Mostly a legal question; the daughter's reaction is not told.

20.actor: A woman divorced by a bill closer to her than to him, and the rabbis
20.event: A bill of divorce was closer to the woman than to the man and was then lost.
20.outcome: After the husband died, they required her to perform halitza rather than rely on the lost bill.
20.summary: Rav Mordekhai told Rav Ashi of a case where a bill of divorce had been closer to the woman and was lost; they still required halitza to be safe.
20.missing: Only a one-line precedent with no details of the people.
